title: Mercy in power
hook: the rulers people still speak of warmly are remembered for mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ordinary believer, the sweeper of the mosque, and the mothers, farmers and traders who carried the faith. Your line was ordinary hands carried it.

A parent at bedtime. A shift manager writing next week's schedule. A teacher holding a red pen over a failing paper. A referee with a whistle. A landlord reading a late-rent text. None of them is a sultan, but each holds a little power over someone else, and chooses every day how to use it. This path has walked past a lot of rulers this year. Ask which of them people still speak of warmly, and a pattern shows up. It isn't the size of the army. Today: mercy in power.
screen: `A PARENT, A MANAGER, A REFEREE.` → `EVERYONE HOLDS A LITTLE POWER.` → `WHICH RULERS ARE SPOKEN OF WARMLY?`

segments.voice: Go back to two names from earlier this year. Salah al-Din, who retook Jerusalem and let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who began his reforms with his own family's wealth. What people still retell is the mercy. Second, the Qur'an puts mercy at the root of leadership. After the battle of Uhud, when some of the companions had failed the Prophet, a verse speaks to him, in Pickthall's translation: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." The same verse tells him to pardon them, to ask forgiveness for them, and to consult them. Not to punish: to keep them close and keep listening. Third, a hadith brings this into every household. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says each of you is a shepherd, responsible for the flock: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's household, a servant for what his master left in his care. Small power is still power. Fourth, a hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One above will be merciful to you. The red pen, the schedule, the whistle: each one a small throne. And the history suggests what will be remembered from it.
screen: `SALAH AL-DIN AND UMAR: THE MERCY IS TOLD.` · `LENIENT, OR THEY WOULD HAVE SCATTERED.` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · `THE MERCIFUL ARE SHOWN MERCY.` · then, large: `IT WAS BY THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself where you hold a little power over someone, a child, an employee, a student, a person waiting on your reply, and picture the next moment you'll have a choice about them: a mistake to correct, a request to answer, a deadline to enforce. Don't drop the standard; just see what a lenient answer would look like, the kind that keeps them close.
Mercy in power. Leniency and pardon from the one who could punish, the thing people remember of their rulers. Today's word.
Your line: mercy is remembered. Leniency is what keeps people close. Day one thousand fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for a flock, and the Qur'an's praise of the Prophet's leniency, when speaking about how parents, employers and leaders should treat those in their care.

chat.says: What did the Qur'an praise in how the Prophet led his companions?
options: His leniency: had he been harsh, they would have scattered.
His strictness: he punished every failure so none repeated it.
His distance: he decided alone, without consulting anyone.
chat.meaning: Qur'an 3:159: by God's mercy he was lenient; had he been stern they would have dispersed. It tells him to pardon and consult them.

notes: Pickthall 3:159 quoted from memory (matches wording used elsewhere on this path); confirm. The rest of the verse (pardon, ask forgiveness, consult) is paraphrased.
The setting of 3:159 after Uhud follows the classical commentaries; confirm phrasing 'some of the Prophet's companions had failed him'.
Bukhari 893 and Tirmidhi 1924 paraphrased; confirm numbers.
Salah al-Din (day 957) and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (day 907) are referred back to with the index wording of those days only; no new historical claims.
Index hook says 'the best rulers are remembered for mercy'; the script avoids the superlative and frames it as 'what people still tell'.
Editor: shepherd hadith (Bukhari 893) brought closer to its wording: 'a woman for her husband's household, a servant for his master's property', replacing 'a worker'.

Audit: 'let people ransom out or leave in peace' overstated 1187: leaving was by ransom, and many who could not pay were taken captive (some were freed without ransom). Now 'let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword'; match pair aligned. 'Their battles and budgets are footnotes now' (an unsourced sweep, and Umar II is not known for battles) softened.
